title: Cross-Cutting
objective: After this level you can explain how cutting between two lines of action happening at once builds suspense.
summary: Crosscutting alternates lines of action in different places at once. Griffith's rescues, as in The Girl and Her Trust (1912), built suspense with ever shorter shots.

cards.headline: A robber escapes, a rescuer gives chase, and you get to watch both.
cards.body: Show only the robbers and you'd wonder where help was. Show only the rescuer and you'd wonder where the robbers were. Cut back and forth between them, and you know exactly how close the rescue is, and how far it still has to go. That knowledge is what builds suspense.

cards.headline: Two places, one clock
cards.body: Cutting between lines of action is called crosscutting, or parallel editing: shots of two or more actions, in different places and usually happening at the same time, alternate on screen, linking them. You met an early example in Level 8, when Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train. Each line of action makes you think about the other.

cards.headline: The ride to the rescue
cards.body: D. W. Griffith became famous for crosscutting in the last-minute rescues that climax his films. In The Girl and Her Trust (1912), robbers escape with the heroine on a railroad pump car while the hero chases them by train. Griffith cuts from one to the other and back. Pump car, train, pump car, train: the gap is closing, but is it closing fast enough?

cards.headline: Shorter shots, faster pulse
cards.body: Intercutting the two lines of action creates the suspense. Then Griffith sped it up by shortening the shots as the chase went on, so the cuts come quicker and quicker until the lines meet. The pace of the cutting becomes your pulse. Crosscutting became a foundation of storytelling on film.

options.label: Two angles on the same conversation
Color and black-and-white footage
options.rationale: Crosscutting is about lines of action, not film stock.

options.label: A scene and its establishing shot
options.rationale: An establishing shot opens a scene; it is not a second line of action.

options.label: Two lines of action in different places

questions.explanation: This technique alternates shots of actions in different places, usually happening at the same time.

questions.prompt: How can crosscutting make a chase feel faster as it nears its end?

options.label: Shorten the shots, so the cuts come quicker
Crank the camera more slowly
options.rationale: The pace comes from the editing, not the camera speed.

options.label: Add a narrator to count down
Switch to one long, unbroken shot
options.rationale: The opposite: more cuts, closer together.

questions.explanation: Intercutting creates suspense, and shortening the shots as the chase goes on, as Griffith did, speeds up the pace.

questions.prompt: In Level 8, Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up operator and the bandits. What is that technique called?

options.label: Match on action
options.rationale: That carries one movement across a cut.

options.label: Shot/reverse shot
options.rationale: That alternates characters in a conversation.

options.label: The stop trick
options.rationale: That's Méliès's camera trick from Level 7.

questions.explanation: Cutting between two lines of action happening at the same time in different places is crosscutting.
